claims.text: Session lengths are nearly identical across both departments, with Easy averaging 12.16 minutes and Hard averaging 11.78 minutes.
Across 2,000 visitors, session minutes are similar in both departments and the overall median sits at 9.80 minutes, well below the mean, suggesting a skewed distribution pulled up by longer sessions.
Some session minutes values were flagged as outliers and kept in the data, so the averages may be influenced by a small number of unusually long sessions.
The Easy department averages 12.16 session minutes and the Hard department averages 11.78 session minutes — a very small difference across 2,000 visitors.

Overall, session minutes range from 0.1 to 75.30, and the median of 9.80 is notably lower than the mean of 11.97, indicating that most sessions are short but a handful of very long sessions pull the average up.
No data was lost during cleaning — all 2,000 rows were retained with no logged changes — so the department averages rest on the full dataset.

Investigate the longest sessions (up to 75.30 minutes) to determine whether they represent genuine engagement or data errors before using averages in reporting. Outliers are kept in the data and may be distorting department-level means

Collect additional attributes (e.g., content type, visitor role) to understand what drives session length within each department. Department alone explains almost no variation in session length given the near-identical averages

Prioritise Enterprise plan retention and expansion efforts, given it contributes the largest share of monthly recurring revenue. Protecting the highest-revenue plan limits downside risk from contraction.

Enterprise leads all plans in total monthly recurring revenue, with Basic at the bottom and Pro in between.
Overall monthly recurring revenue has pulled back from its peak, and net revenue retention has declined year over year, so plan-level trends deserve close attention.

The overall numbers favour control, yet every individual department tells the opposite story, meaning the aggregate result is misleading and the rollout decision cannot safely rest on it.
The conflict between the combined result and the per-department results must be resolved before any rollout recommendation can be made.

Within the Easy department, treatment converts at 0.8 versus control at 0.7; within the Hard department, treatment converts at 0.3 versus control at 0.2 — treatment leads in both departments.
This reversal between the overall and per-department results is a sign that department composition is unevenly distributed across the two groups, making the aggregate comparison unreliable.

Investigate how visitors were assigned to control and treatment groups to determine whether the department mix is balanced between them before drawing any rollout conclusion. Unbalanced assignment is the most likely cause of the conflicting signals and must be ruled out first.

claims.text: Recurring revenue stands at $40,308.46 as of 31 Oct 2026, up 6.5% year-over-year but down 8.0% from its Sep 2026 peak of $43,813.56.
All 200 customers are retained with zero logo churn, and net revenue retention of 106.5% confirms the base is still growing in aggregate.
The month-over-month decline and a net revenue retention rate that has fallen from 122.7% to 106.5% year-on-year signal that expansion momentum is slowing and warrants close attention.
Monthly recurring revenue fell 20% year over year, and it also fell 8.0% in October 2026 compared with September 2026.
The entire $40,308.46 base is driven by expansion MRR of $16,056.28 offset by contraction MRR of $13,587.47 over the past 12 months, with no new, reactivation, or churned MRR in the period.
Net revenue retention has declined from 122.7% (12 months to 31 Oct 2025) to 106.5% (12 months to 31 Oct 2026), a drop of 16.2 points, while gross revenue retention remains strong at 99.3%.

Average monthly recurring revenue varies widely by plan: Enterprise averages $860.39, Pro averages $173.36, and Basic averages $57.97, suggesting the mix of plans is a key driver of overall revenue levels.

Investigate the drivers of contraction MRR ($13,587.47) to identify which accounts downgraded and whether a pattern exists by plan or tenure. Contraction is the sole drag on revenue; reducing it would directly lift net revenue retention back toward prior-year levels.

Develop a pipeline for new customer acquisition, as new MRR contributed $0.00 over the past 12 months. The business currently relies entirely on expansion from existing customers; adding new logos would reduce concentration risk.

Review Enterprise-plan accounts (averaging $860.39 monthly recurring revenue) for upsell and retention risk given the contraction trend. Enterprise accounts represent the highest revenue per customer, so movement in this segment has an outsized effect on total monthly recurring revenue.

claims.text: Support tickets and monthly recurring revenue show no meaningful relationship in this dataset.

Across 6,000 snapshots covering 200 customers, support tickets and monthly recurring revenue move together only negligibly, making it unlikely that ticket volume is a reliable signal of revenue health.
The more notable revenue story is that net revenue retention has declined and contraction MRR is the primary drag on growth.

Support tickets range from 0 to 11 with a median of 3, while monthly recurring revenue ranges from $35.44 to $1,023.37 with a median of $87.35 — the wide spread in revenue with no corresponding pattern in tickets reinforces that the two are unrelated.

Enrich the dataset with ticket category, severity, or resolution time and re-run the analysis to test whether a specific ticket type relates to revenue changes. Raw ticket counts show no signal; a more granular ticket attribute might reveal a relationship that volume alone cannot.

claims.text: This dataset covers 4,203 inpatient stays across 12 months, with a 30-day readmission rate of 9.0%, in-hospital mortality of 2.4%, and an average length of stay of 3.72 days.
Cardiology accounts for the largest share of total charges among all departments, while total charges fell sharply in Oct 2026 compared with Sep 2026.
Cardiology's higher readmissions were caused by poorer care in the department, so its discharge planning should be overhauled.
The dataset contains 4,203 stays from 1,707 patients; Vascular Surgery had only 7 stays, with 2 deaths among its patients.
Cardiology generated the highest total charges ($51,663,189.13), followed by Orthopedics ($33,207,578.70) and General Medicine ($24,167,064.42).

Total charges fell 26.3% from Sep 2026 to Oct 2026; because the data covers only 12 months with no prior-year equivalent, it is not possible to determine whether this is seasonal or a genuine decline.
Per-stay charges vary widely, and three patients were readmitted twice within one week of discharge.

Investigate the drivers of the Oct 2026 drop in total charges before drawing conclusions or adjusting budgets. A 26.3% month-over-month fall is material; confirming whether it is seasonal or structural prevents misinformed planning.

Review the small number of stays with very high charges (up to $827,622.78) to confirm they are coded correctly and assess their effect on departmental totals. Outliers flagged in Total Charges could distort department-level comparisons and financial forecasts.

Risk-adjust the 9.0% readmission rate and 2.4% mortality rate before using them for benchmarking or performance reporting. Crude rates can mislead if case mix differs across departments or time periods.

claims.text: This P&C insurance dataset covers 1,300 policies across Auto and Home lines, with $4,023,883.78 in earned premium and a 51.2% loss ratio over a 46-month period ending October 2026.
Auto is the larger line by both earned premium and incurred losses, while Home is smaller on both measures.
Losses for 2025 and 2026 are final, so the 60.5% loss ratio can be compared directly with earlier years.
Auto's losses are driven by its female policyholders, so raising auto rates for women would bring the Auto loss ratio down.
The portfolio's overall loss ratio is 60.5% on $2,433,528.68 in incurred losses, with 304 claims across 1,300 policies; losses are case-incurred with no IBNR and no loss-adjustment expense included.
Incurred losses are highly skewed: the median per row is $0 while the mean is $910.07 and the maximum reaches $96,357.19, reflecting that most rows carry no loss and a small number carry large ones.
Earned premium ranges from -$3,958.90 to $8,052.87 per row, with a median of $1,415.89; negative values may reflect mid-term cancellations or endorsements and warrant a closer look.

Investigate rows with negative earned premium to confirm they represent valid cancellations or endorsements rather than data errors. Ensures the $4,023,883.78 premium base is reliable before any rate or reserving work.

Obtain a valuation date and add IBNR before using 2025 or 2026 loss figures for pricing or reserving decisions. Prevents understated loss ratios from driving inadequate rates on still-developing years.
Segment the 304 claims by line and policy year to understand where the large losses (up to $96,357.19) are concentrated. Focuses underwriting and reinsurance review on the highest-severity exposures.

Headcount is the people in force at the latest date (contractors and agency workers out, interns and part-timers in); separations and hires are events (a rehire's exits count separately); attrition is separations ÷ the average of the month-end headcounts over the 12 months to that date. Gender is shown as a description only: hiring, firing or pay decisions on it are discrimination, so no recommendation is made on it; groups of fewer than 11 people are not shown.
Ethnicity is special-category data (GDPR Art. 9): shown as a description only, never a recommendation about people, and never for groups of fewer than 11.
Performance ratings describe groups here; they are never used to rank or predict individuals.

Pay is annual base salary as recorded: part-time salaries are not full-time equivalents, so groups with more part-timers (often women) show lower pay than on a full-time-equivalent basis, which the unadjusted pay gap uses; pay is never shown for a group of fewer than 11 people.

Performance ratings describe groups here; they are never used to rank or predict individuals.

claims.text: Low pay is driving attrition: Support, the lowest-paid department, loses the most people, so raising Support salaries would cut its attrition.
The surge in total attrition masks a slight fall in voluntary attrition, and a single month — Jun 2026 — accounts for a disproportionate share of exits, concentrated in one department.

Total attrition reached 29.6% in the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026, up from 22.8% a year earlier (+6.8 points), yet voluntary attrition moved in the opposite direction, falling from 16.9% to 15.9% over the same comparison — meaning the rise is largely involuntary.
Attrition so far in 2026 is 26.2%, an annual attrition rate of 31.4% if the pace holds, the highest in four years.
Only 2 women in Legal left this year, both from the same team.
Ten Support employees are flight risks and should be put on retention plans now.

Investigate the Jun 2026 Support department event: determine whether the 62 exits were a planned reduction or unplanned, and document the business rationale. Explains the majority of the attrition spike and informs whether further headcount loss is expected.

Monitor involuntary attrition separately from voluntary attrition in monthly reporting, given they moved in opposite directions over the past year. Prevents the total attrition figure from masking different underlying workforce dynamics.

Review the 5 rows with an ended status but no termination date and the 5 records dated after 31 Oct 2026 to ensure separation counts and attrition figures are complete. Small data gaps could affect the accuracy of the reported 29.6% attrition rate.

claims.text: A workforce of 353 employees is stabilising: the 12-month attrition rate fell to 14.3% by October 2026, down from 20.9% a year earlier.
The dataset covers 24 months of monthly HR snapshots (Nov 2024 – Oct 2026) across 8,220 employees, tracking headcount, pay, hires, and separations.
Hiring 70 people in 12 months is what pushed attrition up to 14.3%: the new joiners left first.
Attrition has improved materially: the 12-month rate to October 2026 is 14.3%, compared with 20.9% for the 12 months to October 2025, a drop of 6.7 points.
The workforce stands at 353 employees (338.40 FTE) as of 31 October 2026, with hires (70) outpacing separations (49) over the past 12 months, indicating net headcount growth.
Average base salary across all records ranges from $34,400.00 to $170,800.00, with a median of $82,700.00 and a mean of $84,622.10; salary outliers at the high end have been flagged but retained.
Average base salary by department ranges from $83,436.67 in Finance to $87,825.00 in Marketing, with Engineering, Operations, and Sales sitting close together in between.

Investigate what changed between the two 12-month periods to understand what is associated with the attrition improvement, and assess whether the conditions driving it are sustainable. Protects the gains already made and informs retention strategy going forward.

Review the high-end base salary outliers flagged in the data to confirm they are correct records before using pay figures in any compensation benchmarking. Prevents skewed averages from distorting pay decisions.
Segment attrition by department to determine whether the overall improvement is evenly distributed or concentrated in one area. Identifies departments that may still carry elevated turnover risk.

Review Enterprise account health, particularly any remaining single-customer concentrations similar to the Feb 2026 churn event. Enterprise holds $631,048.45 of MRR; one departure can equal months of typical churn.

Obtain monthly MRR snapshots to measure expansion, contraction and net revenue retention, which cannot be computed from this subscription list alone. Without those snapshots, the full picture of revenue health — whether existing customers are growing or shrinking — is not visible.

Read as SaaS subscription data (MRR, ARR, paying customers, new MRR, churned MRR, logo churn). MRR is the monthly run-rate of the customers paying at the latest date (an annual plan ÷ 12, net of discounts; trials, paused and unpaid subscriptions out, past due in), not revenue; movements and retention compare each customer's MRR at month-ends over the 12 months to that date, and annual churn is measured on the customers paying 12 months earlier, never a monthly rate × 12. A customer who starts and leaves inside one month appears in no month-end figure.
The cancellation date in this export is when a customer asked to cancel, not when the subscription ended: a subscription keeps paying until its end date (or a scheduled cancellation date).
Some subscriptions are scheduled to cancel after the latest date: they are still paying and are counted until they end.

On a subscription list, MRR is computed by the product from each subscription's price, seats, discount and billing interval, at today's price: expansion, contraction and revenue retention need monthly MRR snapshots and are not computed from it.

Read as SaaS subscription data (MRR, ARR, paying customers, new MRR, churned MRR, logo churn, net revenue retention, gross revenue retention). MRR is the monthly run-rate of the customers paying at the latest date (an annual plan ÷ 12, net of discounts; trials, paused and unpaid subscriptions out, past due in), not revenue; movements and retention compare each customer's MRR at month-ends over the 12 months to that date, and annual churn is measured on the customers paying 12 months earlier, never a monthly rate × 12. A customer who starts and leaves inside one month appears in no month-end figure.

claims.text: MRR grew to $562,608.85 (ARR $6,751,306.20) across 539 active customers as of 31 Oct 2026, with Enterprise segment contributing the largest share of total MRR at $322,230.94, followed by Mid at $179,558.89 and SMB at $60,819.02.

The business grew MRR from $412,929.08 to $562,608.85 over the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026, driven by $176,207.56 in new MRR and $89,367.79 in expansion, but gross revenue retention of 77.2% and logo churn of 20.1% point to a retention problem that deserves attention.
The Enterprise price increase caused the March 2026 churn spike ($45,479.75), when Northwind left after its renewal was repriced.

MRR grew to $562,608.85 (ARR $6,751,306.20) across 539 active customers as of 31 Oct 2026, with Enterprise segment contributing the largest share of total MRR at $322,230.94, followed by Mid at $179,558.89 and SMB at $60,819.02.
Annual logo churn is 27.9% (monthly churn of 2.3% × 12), so more than a quarter of customers leave each year.
Net revenue retention of 136.2% over the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026 shows expansion more than replaced every dollar lost.

MRR per customer varies widely — median $273.72 against a mean of $1,013.19 and a maximum of $40,000.00 — indicating a skewed customer base where a small number of high-value accounts drive a disproportionate share of revenue.

Investigate the drivers of logo churn, starting with the 131 customers who stopped paying, segmented by plan size and segment A 20.1% logo churn rate is high enough to threaten long-term growth if not addressed

Review Enterprise account concentration risk and establish early-warning monitoring for large single-customer MRR exposure One Enterprise customer drove 88% of the largest churn month; a repeat event would materially move the MRR bridge

Analyse expansion patterns in the Mid and SMB segments to identify whether upsell motions can improve gross revenue retention beyond 77.2% Closing the gap between gross and net retention would reduce dependence on new customer acquisition to sustain growth
